## This week’s sociological question

<div class="chapter-question">What kind of evidence does an interview produce, and what changes when a model can choose or write the next probe?</div>

## Connection to the preceding material

Week 5 generated fixed candidates before participants encountered them. In an adaptive interview, the participant’s answer changes what comes next. The experimental treatment, data-collection instrument and interaction are now entangled.

## Learning outcomes

You should be able to distinguish interview purposes and survey modes; explain specificity, range, depth and personal context in the focused interview; distinguish speech-to-text, a text interviewer and text-to-speech; compare an assigned protocol with the path a participant actually received; and audit the source and target of every adaptive probe.

## Essential readings and what each contributes

::: {.reading-list}
- **Methods:** Merton and Kendall (1946), “The Focused Interview,” *American Journal of Sociology* 51(6): 541–557. Read the complete article. It supplies foundational criteria for evaluating what a probe elicits. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1086/219886). [@MertonKendall1946]
- **Adaptive survey design:** Velez (2025), “Crowdsourced Adaptive Surveys,” *Political Analysis* 33(4): 284–297. Read the complete article. It shows how respondents’ open-ended answers can become new survey items, and how an adaptive algorithm changes which items later respondents see. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2024.34). [@Velez2025]
- **Methods and LLMs:** Geiecke and Jaravel (2026), “The Rise of AI-Led Interviews in Social Science.” Read the complete paper. It presents a large text-and-voice implementation and explicit validation exercises. [Paper](https://benjamin.geiecke.com/files/ai_interviews.pdf). [@GeieckeJaravel2026]
- **Substantive application:** Rivera (2012), “Hiring as Cultural Matching,” *American Sociological Review* 77(6): 999–1022. Read the complete article. Rivera uses interviews and observation to show how evaluators construct cultural fit in elite hiring; it gives us a real case against which to assess adaptive probes. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1177/0003122412463213). [@Rivera2012]
:::

## Additional readings grouped by purpose

- **For a qualitative chatbot case:** Jack, Cooper and Flower (2026), *Methodological Innovations*. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1177/20597991261448157). [@JackCooperFlower2026]

## Sociological and methodological background

Interviews have never been neutral containers into which respondents deposit attitudes. Merton and Kendall’s focused interview began with a situation the researcher had already analysed and used follow-up questions to recover specificity, range, depth and personal context. A good probe could pursue an unexpected response without telling the respondent what that response ought to mean. Later feminist and reflexive work made power, reciprocity and the interviewer’s social position part of the method. These traditions remind us that the interviewer helps produce the account recorded in the transcript.

Rivera’s study makes the evidentiary stakes concrete. Interviewers described cultural fit, while observation showed how evaluators converted shared tastes and experiences into judgments about candidates. The two sources do not simply duplicate one another. An adaptive interviewer might elicit a specific evaluative episode, but a leading probe could also supply the very explanation the study is meant to discover.

Survey researchers approached interviewing with a different priority: administering comparable questions to many people. CAPI placed the questionnaire on an interviewer’s computer; CASI allowed respondents to answer on screen; audio-CASI read recorded questions aloud. Computerized adaptive tests and branching questionnaires could alter what came next, but usually selected from a question bank written before fieldwork.

Velez changes the timing and source of that question bank. In a crowdsourced adaptive survey, a participant first answers an open-ended question. An LLM converts the answer into a structured survey item; similarity and toxicity checks can prevent unsuitable items from entering the bank; participants rate their own item and items contributed earlier; and a multi-armed bandit changes the probability that each item will be shown in the future. The instrument therefore develops across respondents while the study is running. This is not a free-form qualitative interview: the system creates and prioritizes survey items rather than conducting a turn-by-turn conversation.

Week 6 therefore distinguishes three decisions that are easily collapsed under the word *adaptive*: changing a shared question bank across respondents, selecting a prepared follow-up for one respondent and composing a new probe from the current conversation. Each design requires a different record of what the participant encountered and why.

## Synthesis of the current LLM literature

Velez provides the clearest example of adaptation at the level of the shared instrument. His applications to issue salience, misinformation among Latino respondents and local political concerns recovered participant-generated topics that a fixed researcher-authored battery could miss. The design also creates problems that a conventional fixed survey does not have. Researchers must preserve the source response, the LLM-produced item, the filtering decision, the version of the question bank, participant ratings and the probability with which the adaptive algorithm selected an item. Late-arriving items have had fewer chances to be rated, and an algorithm that prioritizes popular items must still reserve opportunities to test new ones.

AI-led interviewing moves adaptation inside a participant’s conversation. Geiecke and Jaravel’s system conducts both text and voice interviews: in the voice route, speech-to-text produces the transcript read by the language model and text-to-speech voices the next question. Jack and colleagues use a web chatbot built around Gemini Flash 1.5 and study both the interview data and researchers’ experience of the system. Here the record must preserve the conversation available to the model, the exact probe it produced and any human edit or approval. A smooth exchange does not tell us whether the probe was relevant, non-leading or analytically useful.

The comparison gives us two separate validation questions. For Velez, does the generated item accurately represent the participant’s contribution, pass the stated filters and receive a defensible chance of selection? For an AI interview, does the next question improve specificity or coverage without inserting a cause, repeating an earlier question or closing down an unexpected account? Completion rate and conversational fluency answer neither question. In the worked example, the check is deliberately substantive: does the follow-up ask an evaluator to describe a concrete hiring decision, or does it prematurely name “cultural fit” as the cause?

Both designs also make infrastructure part of the method. Audio may pass through a transcription service; transcripts and prompts may be sent to a model provider; an adaptive survey must store participant-generated items while the study is active. Researchers therefore need to specify which service receives which data, how long those data are retained, who owns the resulting question bank or transcript and whether the material is reused. Local models can reduce external transfer, but require suitable hardware, model files, maintenance and usually slower inference.

## Summary and preparation for next week

An adaptive interviewer produces different question paths from the same protocol. After the midterm break, Week 7 moves from asking people questions to asking a model to answer as if it were a person.
